name: Mota
confidence_why: Codrington 1885, the only first-hand grammar of Mota, puts stress on the first syllable of two-syllable words and has each stem or affix keep its own accent in longer words, and Clark 2009 repeats the two-syllable rule, but an uncited modern statement that Mota has no stress at all stands against it and no modern phonological description of Mota exists to settle the question.
catalog_citation: Codrington, R.H. 1885. The Melanesian Languages. Oxford: Clarendon Press. Part III Melanesian Grammars, I. Banks' Islands, 1. Mota.
catalog_locator: pp.253-254, 'Accent' paragraph of the Mota grammar (archive.org, text)
catalog_quote: Accent. — It cannot be said that the accent usually falls on any one syllable, except in words of two syllables, in which the stress is on the first. It is certain that the incidence of the accent on one syllable does not, as in English, obscure the vowels in other syllables; if the accent is on the first syllable in manigiu it does not prevent the full sounding of the succeeding i. In compound words, and words with affixes, the members of the compound, or the stems, retain their natural accent; tdno matur a sleeping place, gasdl a knife, mawora broken, maworavag break with. In fact, the accent falling on the latter syllable is a safe guide to the character of the words — ga-sal from sal to cut, ma-tur from the prefix ma and the root represented by the Malagasy turi. The accent in such words as nasasdna, ravevena falls distinctly on the penultimate, for the reason that sasa, veve are …

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the deciding 'Accent' paragraph is verbatim in the held archive.org text of Codrington 1885 at the stated place (lines 22051-22072, page break to p.254 inside the passage). (2) Deciding source: an 1885 first-hand grammar sketch by the principal authority on Mota; Glottolog's entire descriptive bibliography for Mota is Codrington (1877, 1885, 1896), all held, and only 1885 speaks to accent. Web search (JIPA, LangSci, SIL, ANU/Pacific Linguistics, Pangloss, dissertations) found no modern grammar or phonology of Mota; modern mentions are historical-comparative (François 2005, held, no synchronic Mota stress statement; Clark 2009, downloaded, p.22 'Stress is on the first syllable of a two-syllable word', which matches our secondary rule and is silent on the morphological part).
